name: Chopta Valley
tagline: A high meadow beside the Lachen river, just beyond Thangu
meta_description: Chopta Valley, North Sikkim: high meadow at about 4,000 m near Thangu. Summer flowers, winter ice, add-on cost from Lachen, permits and altitude tips.
summary: Chopta Valley is a high, open meadow at about 4,000 m along the Lachen river near Thangu, about 30–35 km above Lachen. It flowers in summer and turns white and icy in winter. Visited as a short add-on on the Gurudongmar trip when permitted, it is also a gentler alternative for those not going to the lake.
intro: Chopta is a broad stretch of the upper Lachen valley just beyond Thangu, where the river runs through flat meadow between steep, bare slopes. In summer the grass is green and full of alpine flowers, yaks graze, and the river runs clear. In winter the meadow lies under snow and the river edges freeze, a landscape that looks closer to the Tibetan plateau than the forested valleys below.

Most travellers see Chopta for a few minutes from the vehicle on the way to or from Gurudongmar. Some drivers offer a short detour into the valley on the return, for about ₹1,500–2,500 per vehicle, but whether it is allowed depends on army and permit rules that day. We treat it as a welcome extra, never a fixed part of the plan.

At about 4,000 m, Chopta is high, though about 1,150–1,400 m lower than Gurudongmar. For families with older parents or travellers who do not feel well enough for the lake, a gentle hour at Chopta can be the better choice: big views, fewer risks. Walk slowly, keep warm and stay at the road edge.

story.title: Hooker's road to the Tibetan passes
story.text: In 1849 the British botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker travelled up the Lachen valley, past the place he called Tungu, now Thangu, towards the high passes on the Tibetan frontier. His Himalayan Journals, published in 1854, describe the change from forest to open, wind-scoured pasture above Thangu, the yak herders, and the plants he collected in the alpine meadows, among them primulas, saxifrages and dwarf rhododendrons. Wikipedia's article on Tso Lhamo notes that Hooker referred to that lake as Cholamoo, and his route took him into the high country beyond Chopta. He was there as a scientist, and his journals, though written from a colonial viewpoint, remain one of the earliest detailed descriptions of the upper Lachen valley and its people. Today the valley Hooker walked through is crossed by the road to Gurudongmar, and much of the country beyond is restricted. Chopta is where you can still stand in the kind of meadow he described: open grass, cold wind, herds on the slopes, and snow peaks close above.
story.source: Hooker, Himalayan Journals (1854); Wikipedia, Tso Lhamo Lake

little_known.fact: Wikipedia often pairs the names as Thangu-Chopta Valley, since the Chopta meadows begin just beyond Thangu village on the Lachen river.
Chopta lies at roughly 13,000–13,100 ft (about 4,000 m), more than 1,100 m below the official altitude figure for Gurudongmar Lake.
Wikipedia describes Chopta as rich in alpine flora and rhododendrons, with rivers and grazing grounds used by herders of the Lachen valley.

facts: ≈ 155 km · via a night in Lachen
High meadow, summer flowers, winter ice, yaks
Protected area permit via a registered agent; foreigners ask us

highlights.title: Open meadow by the river
highlights.text: A rare flat valley floor in Sikkim's steep mountains, with the Lachen river winding through. In clear weather the slopes and peaks above make it one of the most open landscapes in the state.

highlights.title: Summer flowers
highlights.text: From late May into July, primulas and other alpine flowers spread across the meadow and slopes. The monsoon season makes roads unreliable, so late May and early June are the safer bet.

highlights.title: Winter ice
highlights.text: From late autumn the river edges freeze and snow covers the meadow. Access depends on the Gurudongmar road being open, which is often not the case in midwinter.

highlights.title: Yaks on the slopes
highlights.text: Herds graze in and around Chopta in the warmer months. Keep a distance, never feed them, and ask herders before taking photographs.

highlights.title: A gentler alternative
highlights.text: For travellers not going to Gurudongmar, a short visit to Chopta offers high-country scenery at a lower altitude, if permitted on the day.

how_to_reach.text: Ask your driver about a Chopta detour on the Gurudongmar trip, usually on the way back. It costs about ₹1,500–2,500 per vehicle when allowed.
In a private registered SUV arranged through an agent, request Chopta in advance; the driver still needs permission on the day.
Drive to Gangtok (4.5–5 hours by NH10, or via Kalimpong when NH10 is closed), stay a night, go to Lachen the next day and visit Chopta on the following morning's Gurudongmar trip.

where_to_stay: There is no tourist accommodation in Chopta Valley. Stay in Lachen, about 30–35 km below, and visit on the Gurudongmar morning. Budget travellers can choose a Lachenpa family homestay with an early breakfast; Summit Gangchen is the comfort choice, with heated beds. Thangu has very basic lodging, but sleeping at about 3,900 m without acclimatisation is not advisable for most visitors.
tips: Ask about the Chopta detour the night before so your driver can plan for it.
Stay on the road edge or obvious paths; the meadow is fragile.
Keep stops short in wind; it is colder than it looks.
Do not photograph army installations in or near the valley.
If you skip Gurudongmar, ask whether a Chopta-only visit is permitted that day.

experiences.title: An hour in the Chopta meadow
experiences.summary: On the way back from Gurudongmar, if permitted, turn into Chopta Valley for a slow walk by the Lachen river through open meadow, with yaks on the slopes and snow peaks above. A calmer, lower coda to the morning.
body: After the cold, windy hour at Gurudongmar, Chopta feels gentle. The road drops back towards Thangu, and a short detour leads into the meadow where the Lachen river winds through grass. Step out, breathe, and walk slowly along the bank. The altitude here is about 4,000 m, so you will still feel it, but much less than at the lake.

In summer the meadow is green and flowering; in October and November it turns gold and brown under clear skies; in winter it may be white with snow and edged with ice. Yaks often graze nearby. Watch from a distance and keep children close.

Whether the detour is allowed depends on rules that day. Ask your driver the night before and agree the cost. If it is not possible, the view of Chopta from the main road on the way down is still worth a short stop.

faqs.q: Is Chopta Valley included in the Gurudongmar trip?
faqs.a: Usually not as a full stop. You pass the valley on the main road, and some drivers offer a short detour for about ₹1,500–2,500 per vehicle. Whether it is allowed depends on army and permit rules that day. Ask the night before.

faqs.q: How long do we get at Chopta?
faqs.a: Typically 30 minutes to an hour on the way back from Gurudongmar. Drivers need to return to Lachen for lunch and continue to Lachung or Gangtok, so the stop is short. A private vehicle allows a little more flexibility.

faqs.q: Is Chopta easier on altitude than Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Yes, it is about 4,000 m, more than 1,100 m lower than the lake. Most people feel better there. It is still high, so walk slowly and keep warm, and descend if someone feels seriously unwell.

experiences.title: Chopta for those not going to the lake
experiences.cost: Vehicle cost as agreed with your agent
experiences.summary: If a family member is too young, too unwell or simply not keen on 5,000 m, Chopta and Thangu make a sensible alternative morning: high-country scenery and fresh air at about 3,900–4,000 m, with a much lower risk of altitude sickness.
body: Gurudongmar is not for everyone. Older parents, people with heart or lung conditions, or anyone who felt unwell in Lachen may be better off stopping lower. Chopta and Thangu give much of the same feeling of leaving the forest for open, high country, without the final climb above 5,000 m.

In a private vehicle you can plan this from the start: a later start from Lachen, breakfast at Thangu, an hour in Chopta, and back to Lachen. In a shared jeep, the person can wait at Thangu and visit Chopta on the return if the driver allows the detour.
Permission for Chopta depends on rules that day, so confirm with your agent in advance. Whatever the plan, follow the same altitude care: water, warmth, a light meal and a slow pace.

faqs.q: Can we visit only Chopta and not Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Sometimes, in a private vehicle, if permits and army rules allow it that day. Ask your agent when booking. In shared jeeps, the group goes to Gurudongmar, so an unwell traveller usually waits at Thangu instead.

faqs.q: Is Chopta suitable for senior citizens?
faqs.a: More so than Gurudongmar, since it is much lower. Seniors in reasonable health usually manage a short, gentle visit. Consult a doctor first if you have heart, lung or blood pressure conditions, and keep the stop short and warm.

faqs.q: Can children visit Chopta Valley?
faqs.a: Children aged five and over can, with care; children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas. For children who may struggle at Gurudongmar, Chopta is a lower, gentler alternative. Watch for headache or vomiting.

experiences.title: Snow and ice in Chopta Valley
experiences.best_time: Late October to December, when the road is open
experiences.summary: From late autumn, snow covers the Chopta meadows and ice forms along the Lachen river. When the Gurudongmar road is open, the white valley under clear November skies is one of North Sikkim's starkest and most beautiful scenes.
body: As temperatures drop in late October and November, Chopta changes quickly. Frost whitens the grass at dawn, the river edges freeze, and the first snowfalls cover the meadow. Clear post-monsoon skies make the colours sharp: blue sky, white snow, brown slopes.

Access depends on the Gurudongmar road. In November it is usually open, though cold; from December snow often closes it. Lachen trips may be cancelled at short notice, so treat winter Chopta as a bonus if it happens.
Dress for well below freezing with wind: thermals, a down jacket, cap, gloves and sunglasses. Ice near the river is slippery and unstable, so stay on solid ground and never walk onto frozen water.

faqs.q: Does the river in Chopta freeze?
faqs.a: The edges and slower stretches often freeze from late autumn through winter, and the meadow is covered in snow. The main current may keep flowing. Never walk on river ice; it is thin and unpredictable.

faqs.q: Is Chopta open in winter?
faqs.a: Only when the Gurudongmar road is open, which is often not the case from December to March due to snow. November is usually the last reliable month. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How cold is Chopta in November?
faqs.a: Mornings are often −10 °C or colder with wind, and days stay below freezing in shade. Sun makes it feel warmer briefly. Wear full winter clothing and limit time outside the vehicle.

experiences.title: In Hooker's footsteps up the Lachen valley
experiences.summary: In 1849 the botanist Joseph Hooker walked up this valley past Thangu towards the Tibetan passes, describing the herders, meadows and plants above the tree line. Read his account and see how much of it you recognise at Chopta.
body: Joseph Dalton Hooker spent 1848–49 exploring Sikkim, and his Himalayan Journals describe the upper Lachen valley in detail. Above the village he called Tungu, now Thangu, he found open, windswept pastures, yak herders and a flora of small, tough alpine plants.

Reading a few pages before your trip changes how you see Chopta. The meadow, the river and the herds on the slopes are recognisably the same landscape, though a road now runs through it and the border beyond is closed. Hooker's view was that of a 19th-century British scientist, but his observations of plants and terrain remain valuable.
The Himalayan Journals are out of copyright and freely available online. Chapters on the Lachen valley and the passes give the best background for this stretch of road.

faqs.q: Where can I read Hooker's Himalayan Journals?
faqs.a: The Himalayan Journals, first published in 1854, are out of copyright and available free on Project Gutenberg, the Internet Archive and other digital libraries. The second volume covers his travels in northern Sikkim, including the Lachen valley.

faqs.q: Did Hooker visit Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: His journals describe the high country and lakes of the upper Lachen valley and passes on the Tibetan frontier, and he named Tso Lhamo as Cholamoo. We have not confirmed a specific description of Gurudongmar, so we do not claim one.

faqs.q: Why is Hooker important to Sikkim's story?
faqs.a: Hooker's collections and writings introduced Sikkim's rhododendrons and alpine plants to the world, and his journals are among the earliest detailed accounts of northern Sikkim. They are a historical source to read critically, alongside Lepcha and Bhutia histories.

faqs.q: Where is Chopta Valley in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Chopta Valley is in the upper Lachen valley in Mangan district (North Sikkim), just beyond Thangu and about 30–35 km above Lachen, on the road to Gurudongmar Lake. It should not be confused with Chopta in Uttarakhand, a separate place.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Chopta Valley?
faqs.a: About 4,000 m (13,000–13,100 ft). It is a little higher than Thangu and more than 1,100 m below the official altitude figure for Gurudongmar Lake, so it is a gentler stop for most visitors.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Chopta Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. It falls within the protected area covered by the Lachen and Gurudongmar permit, arranged through a registered agent with a registered vehicle. Whether vehicles may enter the valley itself depends on rules that day. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Chopta Valley?
faqs.a: Late May to June for flowers with reasonably open roads, and October to November for clear skies and the first ice. July and August bring the most flowers but the worst roads. December to March often sees the road closed by snow.

faqs.q: How much does the Chopta Valley add-on cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively, about ₹1,500–2,500 per vehicle in 2026, paid to the driver or agent, when the detour is allowed. Agree the price before setting out from Lachen. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Chopta Valley?
faqs.a: Rules for foreign nationals in Lachen and Thangu are unclear at present, and Chopta lies beyond Thangu. Foreigners are not permitted at Gurudongmar. Ask us before planning any foreign traveller's trip on the Lachen side.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere to stay in Chopta?
faqs.a: No. There is no tourist accommodation in the valley. Stay in Lachen and visit on the Gurudongmar morning. Thangu nearby has very basic lodging, but sleeping at that height without acclimatisation is not advisable.

faqs.q: Are there yaks in Chopta Valley?
faqs.a: Yes, often in the warmer months, when herders bring yak and sheep to the high pastures. Sightings are likely from May to November but not guaranteed. Keep a distance, do not feed the animals and ask before photographing herders.

faqs.q: Is Chopta Valley worth it?
faqs.a: If permitted, yes, especially as a calm stop after Gurudongmar or as an alternative for anyone not going to the lake. It is not a destination in itself for most travellers, since there is no accommodation and visits are short.
